title: Can't build Flutter applications on old x86_64 CPUs with 3.16.0 and greater
body: I upgraded from Flutter 3.10 to 3.16.3/3.16.4 on Windows 10. Since then, creating a new project exits with code 3221225501, often immediately after downloading sky_engine, and building for Windows fails through MSBuild with exit code -1073741795. Cleaning the project, repairing or clearing the pub cache, and deleting the Windows folder did not resolve it. Flutter 3.10 worked on this machine. What is causing the crash, and how can I build projects successfully again?

symptoms_visible: After upgrading from Flutter 3.10 to 3.16, flutter create and flutter pub get finish part of their work and then exit with code 3221225501, often just after downloading sky_engine.
Deleting the Windows folder, running flutter clean, and repairing or clearing the Dart pub cache leave the behavior unchanged.
N0.label: N0 Flutter tool exits on old Windows machine

symptoms_visible: After trying the suggestions from the linked MSB8066 thread, Flutter commands still exit with code 3221225501 and new projects still do not build.
N1_x.label: N1_x generic MSB8066 troubleshooting aftermath

symptoms_visible: Fresh installations of Flutter 3.10.5, 3.13.0, and 3.13.9 create and run projects, while fresh installations of 3.16.0 and 3.16.4 exit and fail across platforms on my AMD Phenom II X4 965 machine.
N2_x.label: N2 versions swept

symptoms_visible: Verbose runs on Android, Windows, and web stop while Flutter's cached Dart SDK is executing the frontend tooling, without a useful Flutter exception.
The same abrupt exit is reproducible on several older x86-64 processors, including AMD Phenom II, AMD Athlon II, and Intel Core 2 Quad machines.
N3.label: N3 verbose cross-platform evidence collected

symptoms_visible: The Flutter tool continues to terminate on the affected processors; separate git-bisect runs print first-bad engine-roll commits from July 12–13, 2023.
N4.label: N4 regression narrowed to July 2023 engine rolls

symptoms_visible: Running a one-line Dart program containing 42.0.floor() with the Flutter SDK's normal dart command crashes with -1073741795, but the same command prints 42 when run with --target-unknown-cpu.
The trace-cpuid test reports 'sse41? no' on the affected AMD and Intel processors before the ordinary run crashes.
N5.label: N5 Dart CPU-instruction probe isolates the crash

symptoms_visible: With Flutter 3.19.5 and Dart 3.3.3, projects build and run successfully on the affected older processors.
The Windows test application starts and prints the expected ceil result, and Windows, Android, and browser builds complete normally.
N6.label: N6 stable hotfix verified on affected hardware

symptoms_visible: Flutter commands no longer exit with code 3221225501 on the older x86-64 CPUs, and new applications build and run successfully after updating to Flutter 3.19.5 or later.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved

solution.intent: Treat the failure as a conventional Windows MSBuild MSB8066 project-configuration problem and apply the generic fixes from the linked Stack Overflow thread.
solution.concrete_example: Follow the suggested MSB8066 remedies in the linked Stack Overflow thread, such as repairing the Windows build setup and regenerating project build files.

edges.comment: The reporter had already read the linked thread and then confirmed that its suggested remedies did not change the failure. The later cross-platform and direct-Dart reproductions also show this was not an MSBuild-only problem.

question_patterns: Have you tried a completely clean Flutter SDK reinstall — does anything change?
Does removing and re-downloading the SDK affect the failure?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes — I removed the SDK entirely and re-downloaded it; flutter commands still die the same way.

question_patterns: Could you try a few older Flutter versions and tell me which ones work?
Does 3.13.x work on this machine while 3.16.x fails?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Tried them side by side: 3.10.5, 3.13.0 and 3.13.9 all work; 3.16.0 and 3.16.4 both fail with the same exit code.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Every version I try fails, including 3.10.5 and 3.13.9.

question_patterns: Is this Windows-only, or do Android/web builds fail too?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Not just Windows — new projects fail for Android and web builds as well, same exit.

edges.comment: Re-typed per round-3 audit: the reinstall check and the version sweep are handler-promptable measurements (measurement-class rule), giving N0 a canonical exit; the ancient-CPU blind path stays on e1.

question_patterns: Can you create a fresh project and share full flutter run -v output for Android, Windows, and web?
Where does the verbose run stop on each target?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Ran the failing commands with -v: the Windows build gets through kernel_snapshot and then dies; in each log the process exits while the cached Dart executable is invoking Flutter's frontend tooling.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Only the Windows target fails, and the verbose log shows a missing Visual Studio SDK file; Android and web run normally.
All three targets terminate at the same Dart-tool stage, but my SDK is installed on C: instead of I:.

question_patterns: Does this computer meet Flutter's documented Windows system requirements?
Have you checked the hardware and operating system against the installation requirements?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, I checked the linked requirements and my Windows computer meets the documented Flutter system requirements.

question_patterns: What CPUs are the other affected machines using?
Could the other people hitting this share their processor models?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The others hitting this posted their hardware: Athlon II X4 635, Phenom II X4/X6, and a Core2 Quad — all of us are on older processors.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The other affected machines are brand-new Ryzen and Alder Lake boxes.

edges.comment: The verbose logs were supplied by the original reporter. Reports from additional affected users with AMD Athlon II, AMD Phenom II, and Intel Core 2 Quad CPUs are folded into the target node's volunteered information.

question_patterns: Can you git-bisect the Flutter repository between a working older revision and a failing revision and paste the final output?
Please continue the bisect until Git prints the first bad commit.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: We completed the bisects. One run printed '47ba59c762919d66811b72acab9732d6aa2a93c9 is the first bad commit' for a July 12 engine roll from 16e2ab7e986c to 1b1ccdd1f527. Another run printed 'ee4208fd26abd5c91680b4aa185df0ae9e00ce61 is the first bad commit' for a July 13 engine roll from 16e2ab7e986c to b4080361f2f9.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The bisect ends at a Flutter tool change that only modifies Windows path separators, with no engine or Dart roll in the range.
Both bisects end at adjacent engine-roll commits from the same July 2023 window rather than the two exact hashes reported here.

edges.comment: Two affected users ran the bisects and obtained nearby but different first-bad engine-roll commits; they are folded into one simulated user side. The answer preserves the raw git output. Determining which underlying Dart behavior in those rolls matters is engineer-side inference.

question_patterns: Using the Dart executable from the failing Flutter installation, can you run a program that prints 42.0.floor(), then rerun it with --target-unknown-cpu?
Does the minimal floor.dart program behave differently with --target-unknown-cpu?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: With floor.dart containing `main() { print(42.0.floor()); }`, the normal `dart floor.dart` command crashes with ExceptionCode -1073741795. Running `dart --target-unknown-cpu floor.dart` prints `42`.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both the normal run and the --target-unknown-cpu run print 42 without crashing.
The normal run crashes and the unknown-CPU run prints 42, but I tested Dart 3.3.0 instead of 3.2.5.

question_patterns: Can you run the trace-enabled Dart executable with --trace-cpuid and paste the CPU feature output?
Does --trace-cpuid report SSE4.1 support on the affected processor?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: The trace output identifies our AMD Phenom II, AMD Athlon II, and Intel Core 2 Quad processors and prints `sse41? no sse2? yes`. After that, the ordinary floor.dart execution crashes with -1073741795.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The trace reports `sse41? yes`, and the ordinary floor.dart run still crashes at the same operation.

edges.comment: These are handler-initiated diagnostic measurements performed by several affected users, folded into one simulated user side. The users report only the crash, successful fallback output, and raw CPUID feature result. Inferring that an SSE4.1 rounding instruction was emitted despite the restriction is reserved for the final solution.

question_patterns: Can you update to Flutter 3.19.5 with Dart 3.3.3 and verify that projects build on the affected machine?
Please test the stable hotfix on Windows and rerun the rounding code sample.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I tested Flutter 3.19.5 with Dart 3.3.3 on the affected old CPU. Windows builds successfully and the application runs and prints `ceil result: 1016!`. I also confirmed successful Android and browser runs; everything works normally now.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Flutter 3.19.5 still exits with -1073741795 and the same floor or ceil operation crashes on the old CPU.
Flutter 3.19.5 builds and runs the Windows sample correctly, but I did not retest Android or web.

edges.comment: Verification came from multiple affected users on old AMD and Intel processors, folded into one simulated user side. Installing and exercising the fixed stable version is treated as a verification measurement before resolution is declared. [The 3.19.5 install used for verification persists on the testers' machines (S1->S1b); the terminal edge recommends the fixed stable for the reporter.]

solution.intent: Update to Flutter 3.19.5 or later, which includes Dart 3.3.3 and the CPU-feature restriction fix preventing the Flutter tool's JIT compiler from emitting unsupported SSE4.1 rounding instructions on older x86-64 CPUs.
solution.concrete_example: Install Flutter 3.19.5 or a newer stable release and confirm `flutter --version` reports Dart 3.3.3 or later. The Dart fix closes the JIT CPU-restriction hole that allowed an SSE4.1 `roundsd` operation to be generated on processors reporting no SSE4.1 support.
solution.inference_hint: The users supplied the version boundary, bisect output, crash code, successful --target-unknown-cpu result, and CPUID lines saying SSE4.1 is absent. Engineers connected that evidence to the generated `roundsd` instruction and concluded that Dart's JIT CPU-restriction handling failed to suppress SSE4.1 code generation. That mechanism is inference, not a fact stated by the reporter.

edges.comment: The Dart fix under review 357218 was incorporated into Dart 3.3.3 and shipped in Flutter 3.19.5. Older stable Flutter lines were not separately hotfixed; release coordination itself is not scored.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the root cause as a Dart VM JIT CPU-feature restriction bug that allowed an SSE4.1 rounding instruction such as `roundsd` to be generated on older x86-64 processors that report no SSE4.1 support, causing exception code -1073741795/exit code 3221225501 while the Flutter tool runs.

The diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: the old-CPU and Flutter-version boundary, cross-platform failure inside Dart-powered Flutter tooling, the July 2023 engine-roll bisects, the minimal floor.dart crash, successful `--target-unknown-cpu` run, and `sse41? no` CPUID output.
Must recommend updating to Flutter 3.19.5 or later with Dart 3.3.3 or later rather than treating downgrading to 3.13.9 as the permanent fix.
Must not settle on generic MSB8066 troubleshooting or SDK reinstallation; both were tried in-case without resolving affected Flutter versions.
Must not attribute the root cause to mixed Windows and Unix path separators; the direct one-line Dart reproduction and CPU-feature measurements isolate the failure below project path handling.
Must require successful testing on an affected older CPU before declaring the issue resolved.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Flutter developer on older Windows hardware. Comfortable reinstalling SDK versions, running verbose Flutter commands, checking out Git revisions, and following precise diagnostic instructions, but relies on maintainers to interpret VM crashes and CPU instruction details.
persona_hint.communication_style: Polite, patient, and evidence-oriented. Shares long console outputs, reports exact versions and exit codes, asks focused follow-up questions, and carefully follows requested reproduction steps. Additional affected users with similar old AMD and Intel CPUs are folded into the same simulated user side.
